claims.text: An allowance MAY pin ``body_sha256``. When it does, the acknowledgement applies only to the exact bytes a human reviewed -- a different skill of the same name does not match, and neither does the SAME skill after it is edited, which is the more valuable half.
claims.why: The code checks `if pinned and pinned != identity` and refuses to apply the allowance, matching the claim.

claims.text: An allowance without a pin still works (they are written by hand, and demanding a digest up front would mean nobody writes one) but it is reported as UNPINNED so the weaker form is visible rather than assumed.
claims.why: When `not pinned`, the code appends "[UNPINNED: ...]" to the note, confirming the claim.

claims.text: A pin whose counterpart cannot be computed is a pin that cannot be honoured.
claims.why: When `pinned` and `not identity`, the code refuses the allowance and adds a note about inability to verify.

claims.text: True ONLY for a full scan with nothing found. Everything else — including an unreadable file — is not cleared. This property is the whole fail-closed contract; callers must not re-derive it from ``findings`` being empty.
claims.why: The property returns `self.outcome == CLEAR and not self.skipped`. If there are skipped files, `self.skipped` is non-empty, so `cleared` is False. If outcome is not CLEAR, it's False. This matches the claim.

claims.text: An adversarial review on 2026-07-30 showed why: skills come from several scopes, so a project-scope skill called ``room`` inherited the acknowledgement written for the user-scope ``room`` and its ``subprocess`` call was downgraded from BLOCK to REVIEW. A name is not an identity; anyone who can place a directory can choose one.
claims.why: The claim refers to a historical adversarial review and behavior of allowances across scopes; this code chunk does not contain the allowance lookup or scope handling to verify.

claims.text: An adversarial review on 2026-07-30 broke every exec rule with ``e​val(`` -- the regex sees two tokens, a Python parser sees one identifier, and a MODEL reading the skill sees "eval". Their presence inside source or instructions is itself a signal, so they are stripped for matching AND reported.
claims.why: The comment describes a historical review and behavior of stripping/reporting invisible characters; this chunk only defines the codepoints, not the matching or reporting logic.

observations.what: The `canonical` dictionary is built but its context (function definition) is not in this chunk; it appears to be part of a helper likely named `_canonical_identity`.
The `apply_allowances` function uses `identity` parameter but the docstring claim about pinning refers to `body_sha256`; the code correctly compares `pinned != identity`.

The `_INVISIBLE` constant is defined as a dict.fromkeys but the closing parenthesis is missing in the chunk (line ends with `[0x00AD, 0x200B, 0x200C, 0x200D, 0x200E, 0x200F, 0x2060, 0xFEFF]`). This is likely a truncation; the full definition would include a closing `)`.
The `_worst` function references `_ORDER` which is not defined in this chunk; it is presumably a global dictionary mapping outcome strings to severity integers.
The `Verdict.cleared` property uses `self.outcome == CLEAR`; `CLEAR` is not defined in this chunk, but is presumably a constant imported or defined elsewhere.
